<explanation>
1. Project Type and Purpose  
   - This is an open-source, modular JavaScript/TypeScript library and CLI tool (“Mermaid”) for generating a wide variety of diagrams from plain-text definitions. It is not a monolithic web app but a collection of packages that together provide:  
     • A parser layer for multiple diagram syntaxes (Jison & Langium)  
     • A core “diagram API” that orchestrates parsing, detecting, layout and rendering  
     • Per-diagram modules (flowchart, sequence, class, C4, etc.)  
     • Layout engines (dagre-d3 wrappers and ELK)  
     • A rendering-util layer that emits SVG (and optionally HTML/CSS)  
     • A CLI and Live Editor front end for browser/Node integration  
     • Documentation, tests (Vitest, Cypress, Argos, Applitools) and a build/publishing pipeline (esbuild, Vite, pnpm)

2. Core Components to Show in the Diagram  
   a. User & Entry Points  
     • CLI / Node API / Browser API (mermaidAPI.ts)  
     • Live Editor Web App (demos + .vite server)  
   b. Parser Layer  
     • Jison grammars (per-diagram .jison/parsers)  
     • Langium grammar for custom languages (packages/parser)  
     • parse.ts → AST representations  
   c. Diagram API & Orchestration  
     • diagramAPI.ts / diagram-orchestration.ts  
     • detectType.ts (detects which diagram module to invoke)  
   d. Diagram Modules (for each diagram type)  
     • Detector (e.g., flowDetector.ts)  
     • Database/Model builder (flowDb.ts)  
     • Renderer (flowRenderer.ts, svgDraw.ts)  
     • Styles & icons  
   e. Layout Engines  
     • dagre-wrapper (packages/mermaid/src/dagre-wrapper)  
     • ELK layout (packages/mermaid-layout-elk)  
   f. Rendering-Util Layer  
     • createText.ts, render.ts, insertElementsForSize.js  
     • rendering-elements/shapes (all shape implementations)  
   g. Configuration & Themes  
     • defaultConfig.ts, config.ts  
     • Themes (theme-default.js, theme-dark.js, etc.)  
   h. Packaging & Tooling  
     • Build scripts (esbuild/, .vite/)  
     • CI/CD workflows (.github/workflows)  
     • Publishing pipeline (pnpm, Dockerfile)  
   i. Tests & QA  
     • Unit tests (vitest)  
     • E2E tests (Cypress + Applitools/Argos)

3. Relationships & Data Flow  
   1. User invokes CLI/Browser API →  
   2. Input text flows into Parser Layer → AST  
   3. AST sent to Diagram API → detectType → select Diagram Module  
   4. Diagram Module builds internal model (DB), then requests Layout Engine if needed → layout data  
   5. Model + layout go to Renderer → Rendering-Util → produce SVG/HTML  
   6. Output returned to user (stdout, DOM, file)  

   In parallel:  
   • Configuration reads config objects, directives alter parser/API behavior  
   • Themes/styles are injected at rendering time  
   • Plugins (e.g., JSON-schema, Jison transformer) hook into build/parsing  

4. Key Architectural Patterns  
   - Modular per-diagram architecture with clear “Detector → DB → Renderer” flow  
   - Strategy pattern for multiple layout engines (dagre vs. ELK)  
   - Plugin/hooks in build (esbuild/Vite plugins) and at runtime (preprocess.ts)  
   - Separation of concerns: parsing, orchestration, layout, rendering, theming  

5. Guidelines for an Open-Source Tool Diagram  
   - Emphasize how the core library is extensible via new diagram packages (“packages/mermaid-example-diagram”, “packages/mermaid-zenuml”, etc.)  
   - Highlight plugin points: Jison grammars, Langium grammars, build‐time transformers, JSON-schema generation  
   - Show integration points: how demos, docs, and the Live Editor consume the core library  

6. Diagramming Best Practices  
   - Use distinct shapes/colors:  
     • Blue boxes for core library components (Parser, Diagram API)  
     • Green boxes for per-diagram modules  
     • Orange for layout engines  
     • Purple for rendering-util and themes  
     • Grey for tooling/CI & docs  
   - Draw directional arrows to indicate flow (Text → Parser → API → Module → Layout → Renderer → Output)  
   - Label each arrow with the artifact passed (e.g., “AST”, “Model”, “LayoutData”, “SVG”)  
   - Include boundary markers for “Browser vs. Node vs. CLI” invocation contexts  

7. Level of Detail  
   - Don’t over-fragment: group similar diagram modules under a single “Diagram Modules” cluster, then show example subcomponents  
   - Call out core extension points (packages/parser, plugin directories, build scripts) without listing every file  
   - Ensure the diagram can be read on one page but still shows all essential architectural concerns  

Putting it together, your system design diagram will have:  
   • A leftmost “User & Entry Points” cluster  
   • A central “Core Library” cluster (Parser → Diagram API → Diagram Modules)  
   • A lower “Layout Engines” cluster with conditional arrows from modules  
   • A rightmost “Rendering-Util & Themes” cluster leading to “Output”  
   • Surrounding “Build & Tooling” and “Tests & QA” clusters to show how the repo is maintained and published  

This will clearly convey the core components, their relationships, and the extensibility of Mermaid as an open-source diagramming engine.  
</explanation>
